terms.grammar: demonstrative pronoun and adjective; plural hī, hae, haec
evidence: Catull. 50.16: hoc, jūcunde, tibi poēma fēcī
terms.comment: What is near the speaker, or what has just been said or is about to be. Beside ille it is “this … that”, and of two things just named, “the latter” (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Mart. 4.49.10: laudant illa, sed ista legunt
terms.comment: The demonstrative of the person spoken to: English often says “this” of what the listener holds or has just said. See “that”.

phrases.latin: Hoc facitō. — Rēctē sānē. — Hoc fugitō. — Callidē.
phrases.english: Do this. — Quite right. — Avoid this. — Clever.
I made this poem for you, my dear

phrases.latin: Haec est diēs quam fēcit Dominus; exsultēmus, et laetēmur in eā.
phrases.english: This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.
I wrote this on board ship

phrases.latin: Bonō animō es: accēde ad ignem hunc; jam calēscēs plūs satis.
phrases.english: Cheer up: come over to this fire; you’ll soon be more than warm enough.

phrases.latin: hic tibi nocturnōs praestābit cēreus ignēs
phrases.english: this wax candle will give you light at night

hic.against: Lewis & Short hīc, haec, hōc, marking the heavy syllable as a long vowel
hic.html: De Vaan 284, s.v. hic: the nominative is *hi-ke, so the vowel is short and the syllable heavy (hicc, p. 102, s.v. -ce); the adverb hīc, here, is the old locative *hoi-ke. As in the record for “current”.

sources: Lewis & Short: hic · Lewis & Short: iste
Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), pp. 102, 284.
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-terentius, loci-catullus, loci-vulgata, loci-cicero-epistulae, loci-martialis), checked against the editions named there.
Citations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling, and have not been checked against an edition.
